metadata.title: Root&Remedy — evidence-linked remedy catalog
metadata.intendedAudience: Educational browsing and comparison, with older-adult applicability explicitly recorded.
metadata.description: Twenty scoped remedy records linking preparations, ingredients, cultural associations, health goals, human research, and safety statements to sources.
metadata.sourcePolicy: Every substantive health, preparation, identity, and cultural claim has a source and locator. Primary publications, systematic reviews, government and professional guidance, and botanical or historical references serve distinct roles. Reviewed evidence may be limited or mixed; inclusion is not a treatment recommendation.
limitations: This is a curated research dataset, not an exhaustive systematic review or personalized medical advice.
No clinician has reviewed or approved these records. Public publication remains a separate decision.
All safety scores are null. No validated numerical safety rubric has been applied.
Research volume describes curated coverage, not effectiveness or a ranking of remedies.
Review totals overlap with primary trials and must not be added together. Aggregate participant counts remain null.
Evidence from a particular extract, route, dose, population, or combination does not automatically apply to another product or a homemade preparation.
Older-adult evidence is often indirect or absent. Unknown interaction or population data do not mean no risk.
Cultural associations and botanical ranges are not exclusive countries of invention. Map coordinates remain null pending verified regional geocoding.
Source access varies between full text, abstracts, and summaries. Formal retraction surveillance has not been completed.
Research date is the local America/Los_Angeles date. Sources and recommendations require later review for changes.

claims.text: Capsaicin occurs in chili peppers and is used in topical pain-relief products.
Kew records that many Capsicum annuum varieties were known to Aztecs in Mexico before Spanish arrival.
The ACR/Arthritis Foundation guideline conditionally recommends topical capsaicin for knee osteoarthritis, citing small effects and wide confidence intervals.
NICE’s evidence review advises against routinely offering capsaicin for osteoarthritis because evidence is limited and costs exceed topical NSAIDs.
A 2024 review included eight trials with 498 osteoarthritis patients across topical concentrations and joint sites.
The review suggested pain benefit but noted small samples, short follow-up, heterogeneity, and low-to-very-low certainty overall.
The trial compared 0.025% cream with vehicle on painful knees four times daily for four weeks; participants included 70 with osteoarthritis and 31 with rheumatoid arthritis.
Knee pain relief favored capsaicin over vehicle in the osteoarthritis group; most participants continued other arthritis medicines.
Burning, redness, itching, and irritation can occur. Severe burning, swelling, blistering, or eye pain warrants stopping use and medical advice.

The review found bias concerns, heterogeneous pain-intensity results, and sparse safety reporting; the risk-benefit balance remained unclear.

Pain severity improved versus placebo in both protocols; duration improved significantly only with the five-day protocol.
Oral ginger can cause heartburn, abdominal discomfort, diarrhea, and mouth or throat irritation.
